---
title: "Quiz: images as arrays & geometric transforms"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** A 16-bit greyscale microscopy image has 2048 × 2048 pixels. How many different grey levels can a pixel take, and how many bytes does the image need (uncompressed)?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$2^{16} = 65\,536$ grey levels (0 to 65 535). Each pixel needs 2 bytes, so $2048 \cdot 2048 \cdot 2 = 8\,388\,608$ bytes, i.e. 8 MiB.
:::

---

**Q2.** Without multiplying anything out: what does $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ do to an image? And $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Read the columns: where do $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ go? Then look at the determinant.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$A$ sends $(1,0) \to (0,1)$ and $(0,1) \to (-1,0)$: a rotation by 90° counter-clockwise, $\det A = 1$. $B$ swaps the two axes, $(1,0) \leftrightarrow (0,1)$: a reflection in the line $y = x$, $\det B = -1$, so the image is mirrored.
:::

---

**Q3.** You scale an image by a factor 3 by sending every input pixel to its new position. Why does the result look like a grid of isolated dots, and how do you avoid it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Forward mapping sends the $N^2$ input pixels to $N^2$ positions spread over an area 9 times larger, so 8 of every 9 output pixels receive nothing. Use inverse mapping: for every output pixel $\mathbf{x}'$, look up the input at $A^{-1}\mathbf{x}'$ and interpolate.
:::

---

**Q4.** A transform has $\det A = 0.25$. What happens to the area of a cell in the image? Can you undo the transform?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every area is multiplied by 0.25, so the cell covers a quarter of its original area (for example, scaling both axes by 0.5). It is invertible, since $\det A \neq 0$, so geometrically yes. But when you shrink an image onto the same pixel grid, detail finer than the new pixel spacing is lost, and transforming back cannot restore it.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why does rotating about the image centre need a $3 \times 3$ matrix, while rotating about the origin needs only a $2 \times 2$ one?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A $2\times2$ matrix always keeps the origin fixed, $A\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$. Rotating about another point $\mathbf{p}$ needs a translation: shift $\mathbf{p}$ to the origin, rotate, shift back. Translation is not linear, but it becomes a matrix product in homogeneous coordinates, which are $3\times3$.
:::
